html:
The Mesha Stele is a black basalt stone carved around 840 BCE for Mesha, king of Moab, a kingdom east of the Dead Sea in today's Jordan. It was found at Dhiban in 1868.

Its text, in the Moabite language and an early alphabet close to Hebrew, tells how Mesha threw off the rule of the kingdom of Israel, naming its king Omri, and built towns and roads. It names the god of Israel and is one of the earliest texts outside the Bible to mention Israel. Some scholars read a mention of the house of David in it.

Local people broke the stone after it was found, but a paper squeeze had been taken, and most of it was pieced together. It is now in the Louvre. See also the Phoenician alphabet and Jordan.
